+# Desktop process exit after normal cleanup
+
+Date: 2026-10-02, America/Denver. Active Windows checks ran on October 3 UTC.
+Issue: [#138](https://github.com/vivary-dev/vivary/issues/138)
+Candidate source: `5ce5468c95f3858dce712b89fb4fa135f916fb45`
+Base: `c17a8cae993d6abb3a87c4949b2a047abb462224`
+
+## Change and candidate
+
+The dedicated desktop launcher sets the existing standalone process marker before loading the server. Its lifecycle exits after local-work cleanup and, on success, Nitro close. On this candidate, rejected cleanup waited for other stops before exiting with failure. Hosted lifecycle ownership stays with its host. The desktop's 15-second fallback remained configured, but review subsequently found that Windows failure exit could remove the live server PID needed by `taskkill /T`. Windows failure-fallback preservation remains pending. The [Windows fallback review](https://github.com/vivary-dev/vivary/pull/173#discussion_r4170897427) and [owner handoff](https://github.com/vivary-dev/vivary/pull/173#issuecomment-5964016108) track the separate correction. The successful normal-quit observations below remain evidence for this candidate. This candidate includes the merged #139 scheduler lease patch.
+
+Zo built Workbench and packaged Windows x64 from the same clean source. The ZIP is 222,623,411 bytes with SHA-256 `d8952c3b4c141824ffb3d2d12804f1c82b5d031fb52e30ab486068946f7ae1f3`. Archive integrity passed. Metadata records `sourceDirty: false`, zero tracked overlays, and `commitMatchesPackagedSource: true`. Node is 24.19.0, Electron 44.3.0, and Python 3.12.14. Workbench output remains `prebuilt` with `sourceCommitVerified: false`. The separate clean-source build record supplies that relationship. The verified candidate is a private preview with no release publication.
+
+## Windows observations
+
+Normal window close requested quit. Timing starts at that request. The observer followed candidate process identities.
+
+| Journey | Main process exit | All observed candidate processes gone |
+| --- | ---: | ---: |
+| Earlier `042dce25` idle baseline | 16,359.15 ms | 16,687.44 ms |
+| Combined `5ce5468c` idle | 4,181.73 ms | 4,456.45 ms |
+| Combined `5ce5468c` active scheduled run | 329.85 ms | 582.87 ms |
+| Combined `5ce5468c` active webhook run | 309.92 ms | 559.27 ms |
+
+Every combined observation ended with no surviving candidate process. These measurements establish the named runs, rather than a close-time guarantee. Before both active quits, SQLite held actual running automation and agent rows, and the local gateway recorded an open response stream. Its stream closed during shutdown.
+
+After scheduled quit, the same run was `interrupted` with `background_automation_interrupted` and a non-null finish time. Its agent was `aborted` for `shutdown`. The run lease was deleted. The global scheduler lease's owner and expiry fields were null before and after quit. This observes #139's run-lease release at quit, without establishing its complete two-automation Windows journey.
+
+After webhook quit, the same run was interrupted with that error and its agent aborted for shutdown. The same task changed from `processing` to `pending`. Its `attempts` changed from 1 to 0, refunding the claimed attempt. `dispatch_attempts` stayed 1 and `completed_at` stayed null. This matches Core's existing quit regression that requires a normal quit not to spend an attempt.
+
+## Fixture corrections and verification
+
+The first webhook evidence helper incorrectly required an equal attempt count and reported a false failure. It was corrected against `packages/workbench/tests/automation-quit.test.mjs`, in the case that returns an interrupted webhook call to the queue. Read-only validation of the recorded before and after states passed for both journeys. A control removing persisted interruption was rejected. No application fix or repeated provider call was needed for this correction.
+
+An offline schedule-pause helper failed before mutation because its requested `closeDbExec` export was absent. Pause was not verified, and the schedule remained enabled. The webhook was created and closed before the next launch's first scheduler tick. The recorded state showed one current active webhook run and the previous scheduled run already interrupted.
+
+The actual built server exited normally in 62.09 ms on `5ce5468c`. Three hosted application checks and 43 targeted regressions passed. GitHub reported nine jobs green on that revision, and Entire trail98 recorded one approval. Final CI on the later acceptance documentation commit remains pending and must be reported separately.
+
+## Evidence boundary
+
+The held Builder response was synthetic and loopback. Application startup, SQLite writes, dispatch, interruption, requeue, lease release, and Windows shutdown used the real packaged application. No real provider or tool side effects are claimed. Stuck Windows cleanup was not exercised. The existing controlled regressions did not establish preservation of the Windows fallback after cleanup rejection. That review finding requires separate regression coverage and acceptance.
+
+Webhook relaunch and redelivery, full #139 Windows acceptance, and #140 and #141 remain separate. Historical receipts retain their named-candidate evidence. This receipt does not establish a finished desktop release. Package records, process observations, SQLite snapshots, gateway logs, and corrected validation stay private. No private host path, profile identity, credential, or raw webhook payload is included here.

L32: ## In this article
L33: 
L34: Ends one or more tasks or processes. Processes can be ended by process ID or image name. You can use the cite8†tasklist command command to determine the process ID (PID) for the process to be ended.
L35: 
L36: Note
L37: 
L38: This command replaces the kill tool.
L39: ## Syntax
L40: 
L41:     `taskkill [/s <computer> [/u [<domain>\]<username> [/p [<password>]]]] {[/fi <filter>] [...] [/pid <processID> | /im <imagename>]} [/f] [/t]
L42:     `
L43: ### Parameters
L44: Parameter  | Description
L45: --- | ---
L46: /s `<computer>`  | Specifies the name or IP address of a remote computer (do not use backslashes). The default is the local computer.
L47: /u `<domain>\<username>`  | Runs the command with the account permissions of the user who is specified by `<username>` or by `<domain>\<username>`. The /u parameter can be specified only if /s is also specified. The default is the permissions of the user who is currently logged on to the computer that is issuing the command.
L48: /p `<password>`  | Specifies the password of the user account that is specified in the /u parameter.
L49: /fi `<filter>`  | Applies a filter to select a set of tasks. You can use more than one filter or use the wildcard character (`*`) to specify all tasks or image names. The valid filters are listed in the Filter names, operators, and values section of this article.
L50: /pid `<processID>`  | Specifies the process ID of the process to be terminated.
L51: /im `<imagename>`  | Specifies the image name of the process to be terminated. Use the wildcard character (`*`) to specify all image names.
L52: /f  | Specifies that processes be forcefully ended. This parameter is ignored for remote processes; all remote processes are forcefully ended.
L53: /t  | Ends the specified process and any child processes started by it.
L54: #### Filter names, operators, and values
L55: Filter Name  | Valid Operators  | Valid Value(s)
L56: --- | --- | ---
L57: STATUS  | eq, ne  | `RUNNING | NOT RESPONDING | UNKNOWN`
L58: IMAGENAME  | eq, ne  | Image name
L59: PID  | eq, ne, gt, lt, ge, le  | PID value
L60: SESSION  | eq, ne, gt, lt, ge, le  | Session number
L61: CPUtime  | eq, ne, gt, lt, ge, le  | CPU time in the format HH:MM:SS, where MM and SS are between 0 and 59 and HH is any unsigned number
L62: MEMUSAGE  | eq, ne, gt, lt, ge, le  | Memory usage in KB
L63: USERNAME  | eq, ne  | Any valid user name (`<user>` or `<domain\user>`)
L64: SERVICES  | eq, ne  | Service name
L65: WINDOWTITLE  | eq, ne  | Window title
L66: MODULES  | eq, ne  | DLL name
L67: ## Remarks
L68: 
L69:   * The WINDOWTITLE and STATUS filters aren't supported when a remote system is specified.
L70: 
L71:   * The wildcard character (`*`) is accepted for the `*/im` option, only when a filter is applied.
L72: 
L73:   * Ending a remote process is always carried out forcefully, regardless whether the /f option is specified.
L74: 
L75:   * Providing a computer name to the hostname filter causes a shutdown, stopping all processes.
L76: ## Examples
L77: 
L78: To end the processes with process IDs 1230, 1241, and 1253, type:
L79: 
L80:     `taskkill /pid 1230 /pid 1241 /pid 1253
L81:     `
L82: 
L83: To forcefully end the process Notepad.exe if it was started by the system, type:
L84: 
L85:     `taskkill /f /fi "USERNAME eq NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM" /im notepad.exe
L86:     `
L87: To end all processes on the remote computer Srvmain with an image name beginning with note, while using the credentials for the user account Hiropln, type:
L88: 
L89:     `taskkill /s srvmain /u maindom\hiropln /p p@ssW23 /fi "IMAGENAME eq note*" /im *
L90:     `
L91: 
L92: To end the process with the process ID 2134 and any child processes that it started, but only if those processes were started by the Administrator account, type:
L93: 
L94:     `taskkill /pid 2134 /t /fi "username eq administrator"
L95:     `
L96: To end all processes that have a process ID greater than or equal to 1000, regardless of their image names, type:
L97: 
L98:     `taskkill /f /fi "PID ge 1000" /im *
L99:     `

L291: #### Event: `'disconnect'`cite5†# L292: 
L293: Added in: v0.7.7
L294: 
L295: If the Node.js process is spawned with an IPC channel (see the cite140†Child Process and cite141†Cluster documentation), the `'disconnect'` event will be emitted when the IPC channel is closed.
L296: #### Event: `'exit'`cite6†# L297: 
L298: Added in: v0.1.7
L299: 
L300:   * `code` cite228†<integer>†developer.mozilla.org L301: 
L302: The `'exit'` event is emitted when the Node.js process is about to exit as a result of either:
L303: 
L304:   * The `process.exit()` method being called explicitly;
L305:   * The Node.js event loop no longer having any additional work to perform.
L306: 
L307: There is no way to prevent the exiting of the event loop at this point, and once all `'exit'` listeners have finished running the Node.js process will terminate.
L308: The listener callback function is invoked with the exit code specified either by the cite46†`process.exitCode` property, or the `exitCode` argument passed to the cite45†`process.exit()` method.
L309: 
L310:     [Input]`import process from 'node:process';
L311: 
L312:     process.on('exit', (code) => {
L313:       console.log(`About to exit with code: ${code}`);
L314:     });``process.on('exit', (code) => {
L315:       console.log(`About to exit with code: ${code}`);
L316:     });`[Button: copy]
L317: Listener functions must only perform synchronous operations. The Node.js process will exit immediately after calling the `'exit'` event listeners causing any additional work still queued in the event loop to be abandoned. In the following example, for instance, the timeout will never occur:
L318: 
L319:     [Input]`import process from 'node:process';
L320: 
L321:     process.on('exit', (code) => {
L322:       setTimeout(() => {
L323:         console.log('This will not run');
L324:       }, 0);

The current launcher closes its own IPC channel during normal shutdown, which hides any later parent loss. I recommend keeping IPC open and using a separate disconnect handler to arm one bounded fallback, even when shutdown has already begun.

The P2 is valid. **Keep IPC open during graceful shutdown, then give genuine parent loss one bounded fallback owned by the desktop launcher.** An “explicit shutdown requested” flag alone misses a parent that dies after sending that request.

`desktop-server.mjs` currently calls `process.disconnect()` immediately after emitting `SIGTERM`. That makes normal shutdown indistinguishable from parent loss and prevents observing a later parent death.

I recommend these changes:

1. **Remove the launcher’s voluntary `process.disconnect()`.** Keep its message listener and IPC channel until successful exit or the parent’s tree kill. Node manages the IPC channel’s reference through message and disconnect listeners, so this can replace the lifecycle’s indefinite interval. [Node IPC reference documentation](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v24.x/api/process.html#processchannelref)

2. **Handle disconnect outside the `stopping` guard.** The disconnect handler first arms one referenced Windows fallback timer, then calls the existing idempotent `requestShutdown()`. It must arm that timer even when `stopping` is already true. Thus both initial parent loss and parent loss during cleanup are covered.

3. **Remove the lifecycle’s interval.** Retain successful `process.exit(0)` and Windows desktop failure-exit suppression. While the parent is connected, IPC preserves the root for its existing 15-second fallback. After disconnect, the launcher’s one-shot timer preserves it for bounded cleanup.

4. **At the orphan deadline, attempt exact-own-root tree termination.** Use the absolute system `taskkill.exe`, argument array `["/PID", String(process.pid), "/T", "/F"]`, hidden window, and bounded execution. If the command returns without killing the server, log the failure and exit nonzero rather than retaining it forever. Successful cleanup exits before this timer fires.

A self-tree kill stays scoped to the current server and its descendants, with no PID-reuse window for the root while the server executes. Microsoft documents `/T` as including the specified process’s children. However, its documentation does **not** establish the behavior of a `taskkill` subprocess terminating its own ancestor tree. The native Windows regression must prove that exact arrangement before accepting it. [Microsoft taskkill documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/taskkill)

The regression should distinguish these cases:

- Parent remains connected, cleanup rejects: server stays alive for the parent’s existing tree fallback.
- Parent disappears before shutdown, cleanup remains pending: server and descendant terminate within the orphan bound.
- Parent disappears after requesting shutdown, cleanup rejects or remains pending: the disconnect handler still arms the fallback.
- Parent disappears, cleanup succeeds: ordinary exit occurs before the fallback.

Use an actual intermediary parent process for the abrupt-parent test. Terminate only that parent, without `/T`, so the test does not clean up the server itself. The server’s descendant should retain the existing ignored-stdio and `unref()` arrangement. Final test cleanup must remain outside the measured assertions.

This needs no new environment flag, global registry, or repeating timer. If Windows refuses the self-tree kill, bounded nonzero exit solves the permanent server hang but does not prove descendant cleanup. Record that limit rather than claiming successful cleanup.

L273:     npm audit [fix|signatures]
L274: ## cite203†Description L275: 
L276: The audit command submits a description of the dependencies configured in your project to your default registry and asks for a report of known vulnerabilities. If any vulnerabilities are found, then the impact and appropriate remediation will be calculated. If the `fix` argument is provided, then remediations will be applied to the package tree.
L277: 
L278: The command will exit with a 0 exit code if no vulnerabilities were found.
L279: Note that some vulnerabilities cannot be fixed automatically and will require manual intervention or review. Also note that since `npm audit fix` runs a full-fledged `npm install` under the hood, all configs that apply to the installer will also apply to `npm install` -- so things like `npm audit fix --package-lock-only` will work as expected.
L280: By default, the audit command will exit with a non-zero code if any vulnerability is found. It may be useful in CI environments to include the `--audit-level` parameter to specify the minimum vulnerability level that will cause the command to fail. This option does not filter the report output, it simply changes the command's failure threshold.
L281: ## cite204†Package lock L282: 
L283: By default npm requires a package-lock or shrinkwrap in order to run the audit. You can bypass the package lock with `--no-package-lock` but be aware the results may be different with every run, since npm will re-build the dependency tree each time.
L284: ## cite205†Audit Signatures L285: 
L286: To ensure the integrity of packages you download from the public npm registry, or any registry that supports signatures, you can verify the registry signatures of downloaded packages using the npm CLI.
L287: 
L288: Registry signatures can be verified using the following `audit` command:
L289: 
L290:     $ npm audit signatures
L291: The `audit signatures` command will also verify the provenance attestations of downloaded packages. Because provenance attestations are such a new feature, security features may be added to (or changed in) the attestation format over time. To ensure that you're always able to verify attestation signatures check that you're running the latest version of the npm CLI. Please note this often means updating npm beyond the version that ships with Node.js.
L292: To include the full sigstore attestation bundles in JSON output, use:
L293: 
L294:     $ npm audit signatures --json --include-attestations
L295: 
L296: This adds a `verified` array to the JSON output containing the attestation bundles (DSSE envelopes, verification material, and transparency log entries) for each verified package.
L297: 
L298: The npm CLI supports registry signatures and signing keys provided by any registry if the following conventions are followed:
L299:   1. Signatures are provided in the package's `packument` in each published version within the `dist` object:
L300: 
L301:     "dist":{
L302: 
L303:       "..omitted..": "..omitted..",
L304: 
L305:       "signatures": [{
L306: 
L307:         "keyid": "SHA256:{{SHA256_PUBLIC_KEY}}",
L308: 
L309:         "sig": "a312b9c3cb4a1b693e8ebac5ee1ca9cc01f2661c14391917dcb111517f72370809..."
L310: 
L311:       }]
L312: 
L313:     }
L314: 
L315: See this cite228†example†registry.npmjs.org of a signed package from the public npm registry.
L316: The `sig` is generated using the following template: `${package.name}@${package.version}:${package.dist.integrity}` and the `keyid` has to match one of the public signing keys below.
L317:   2. Public signing keys are provided at `registry-host.tld/-/npm/v1/keys` in the following format:
L318: 
L319:     {
L320: 
L321:       "keys": [{
L322: 
L323:         "expires": null,
L324: 
L325:         "keyid": "SHA256:{{SHA256_PUBLIC_KEY}}",
L326: 
L327:         "keytype": "ecdsa-sha2-nistp256",
L328: 
L329:         "scheme": "ecdsa-sha2-nistp256",
L330: 
L331:         "key": "{{B64_PUBLIC_KEY}}"
L332: 
L333:       }]
L334: 
L335:     }
L336: 
L337: Keys response:
L338:   * `expires`: null or a simplified extended cite229†ISO 8601 format†en.wikipedia.org : `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ`
L339:   * `keyid`: sha256 fingerprint of the public key
L340:   * `keytype`: only `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256` is currently supported by the npm CLI
L341:   * `scheme`: only `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256` is currently supported by the npm CLI
L342:   * `key`: base64 encoded public key
L343: 
L344: See this cite230†example key's response from the public npm registry†registry.npmjs.org .
L345: ## cite231†Audit Endpoints L346: 
L347: There are two audit endpoints that npm may use to fetch vulnerability information: the `Bulk Advisory` endpoint and the `Quick Audit` endpoint.
L348: ### cite206†Bulk Advisory Endpoint L349: 
L350: As of version 7, npm uses the much faster `Bulk Advisory` endpoint to optimize the speed of calculating audit results.
L351: 
L352: npm will generate a JSON payload with the name and list of versions of each package in the tree, and POST it to the default configured registry at the path `/-/npm/v1/security/advisories/bulk`.
L353: Any packages in the tree that do not have a `version` field in their package.json file will be ignored. If any `--omit` options are specified (either via the cite232†`--omit` config , or one of the shorthands such as `--production`, `--only=dev`, and so on), then packages will be omitted from the submitted payload as appropriate.
L354: 
L355: If the registry responds with an error, or with an invalid response, then npm will attempt to load advisory data from the `Quick Audit` endpoint.
L356: The expected result will contain a set of advisory objects for each dependency that matches the advisory range. Each advisory object contains a `name`, `url`, `id`, `severity`, `vulnerable_versions`, and `title`.
L357: 
L358: npm then uses these advisory objects to calculate vulnerabilities and meta-vulnerabilities of the dependencies within the tree.
L359: ### cite207†Quick Audit Endpoint L360: 
L361: If the `Bulk Advisory` endpoint returns an error, or invalid data, npm will attempt to load advisory data from the `Quick Audit` endpoint, which is considerably slower in most cases.
L362: 
L363: The full package tree as found in `package-lock.json` is submitted, along with the following pieces of additional metadata:
L364: 
L365:   * `npm_version`
L366:   * `node_version`
L367:   * `platform`
L368:   * `arch`
L369:   * `node_env`
L370: All packages in the tree are submitted to the Quick Audit endpoint. Omitted dependency types are skipped when generating the report.
L371: ### cite208†Scrubbing L372: 
L373: Out of an abundance of caution, npm versions 5 and 6 would "scrub" any packages from the submitted report if their name contained a `/` character, so as to avoid leaking the names of potentially private packages or git URLs.
L374: However, in practice, this resulted in audits often failing to properly detect meta-vulnerabilities, because the tree would appear to be invalid due to missing dependencies, and prevented the detection of vulnerabilities in package trees that used git dependencies or private modules.
L375: 
L376: This scrubbing has been removed from npm as of version 7.
L377: ### cite209†Calculating Meta-Vulnerabilities and Remediations L378: 
L379: npm uses the cite233†`@npmcli/metavuln-calculator`†npm.im module to turn a set of security advisories into a set of "vulnerability" objects. A "meta-vulnerability" is a dependency that is vulnerable by virtue of dependence on vulnerable versions of a vulnerable package.
L380: For example, if the package `foo` is vulnerable in the range `>=1.0.2 <2.0.0`, and the package `bar` depends on `foo@^1.1.0`, then that version of `bar` can only be installed by installing a vulnerable version of `foo`. In this case, `bar` is a "metavulnerability".
L381: Once metavulnerabilities for a given package are calculated, they are cached in the `~/.npm` folder and only re-evaluated if the advisory range changes, or a new version of the package is published (in which case, the new version is checked for metavulnerable status as well).
L382: If the chain of metavulnerabilities extends all the way to the root project, and it cannot be updated without changing its dependency ranges, then `npm audit fix` will require the `--force` option to apply the remediation. If remediations do not require changes to the dependency ranges, then all vulnerable packages will be updated to a version that does not have an advisory or metavulnerability posted against it.
L383: ## cite210†Exit Code L384: 
L385: The `npm audit` command will exit with a 0 exit code if no vulnerabilities were found. The `npm audit fix` command will exit with 0 exit code if no vulnerabilities are found or if the remediation is able to successfully fix all vulnerabilities.
L386: 
L387: If vulnerabilities were found the exit code will depend on the cite234†`audit-level` config .
L388: ## cite211†Examples L389: 
L390: Scan your project for vulnerabilities and automatically install any compatible updates to vulnerable dependencies:
L391: 
L392:     $ npm audit fix
L393: 
L394: Run `audit fix` without modifying `node_modules`, but still updating the pkglock:
L395: 
L396:     $ npm audit fix --package-lock-only
L397: 
L398: Skip updating `devDependencies`:
L399: 
L400:     $ npm audit fix --only=prod
L401: 
L402: Have `audit fix` install SemVer-major updates to toplevel dependencies, not just SemVer-compatible ones:
L403: 
L404:     $ npm audit fix --force
L405: Do a dry run to get an idea of what `audit fix` will do, and also output install information in JSON format:
L406: 
L407:     $ npm audit fix --dry-run --json
L408: 
L409: Scan your project for vulnerabilities and just show the details, without fixing anything:
L410: 
L411:     $ npm audit
L412: 
L413: Get the detailed audit report in JSON format:
L414: 
L415:     $ npm audit --json
L416: 
L417: Fail an audit only if the results include a vulnerability with a level of moderate or higher:
L418: 
L419:     $ npm audit --audit-level=moderate
L420: ## cite235†Configuration L421: 
L422: ### cite212†`audit-level` L423: 
L424:   * Default: null
L425:   * Type: null, "info", "low", "moderate", "high", "critical", or "none"
L426: 
L427: The minimum level of vulnerability for `npm audit` to exit with a non-zero exit code.
L428: ### cite213†`dry-run` L429: 
L430:   * Default: false
L431:   * Type: Boolean
L432: 
L433: Indicates that you don't want npm to make any changes and that it should only report what it would have done. This can be passed into any of the commands that modify your local installation, eg, `install`, `update`, `dedupe`, `uninstall`, as well as `pack` and `publish`.
L434: 
L435: Note: This is NOT honored by other network related commands, eg `dist-tags`, `owner`, etc.
L436: ### cite214†`force` L437: 
L438:   * Default: false
L439:   * Type: Boolean
L440: 
L441: Removes various protections against unfortunate side effects, common mistakes, unnecessary performance degradation, and malicious input.
L442:   * Allow clobbering non-npm files in global installs.
L443:   * Allow the `npm version` command to work on an unclean git repository.
L444:   * Allow deleting the cache folder with `npm cache clean`.
L445:   * Allow installing packages that have an `engines` declaration requiring a different version of npm.
L446:   * Allow installing packages that have an `engines` declaration requiring a different version of `node`, even if `--engine-strict` is enabled.
L447:   * Allow `npm audit fix` to install modules outside your stated dependency range (including SemVer-major changes).
L448:   * Allow unpublishing all versions of a published package.
L449:   * Allow conflicting peerDependencies to be installed in the root project.
L450:   * Implicitly set `--yes` during `npm init`.

L452:   * Allow unpublishing of entire packages (not just a single version).

**The patch is a credible fix for the reported `max-stale` bypass.** I found no actionable defect in its changed logic. With no published fixed version available, a private scoped vendored fork is the smallest honest replacement I see.

I compared the proposed commit against the published npm 4.2.0 tarball:

- `index.js` differs only by the reviewed security patch.
- `LICENSE` and `README.md` are byte-identical.
- Manifest differences are repository formatting and author-email metadata. There are no added runtime dependencies or install scripts.

The patch checks non-storable responses, `no-cache`, shared-cache `proxy-revalidate`, and restricted shared cookies before allowing stale reuse. It preserves the existing `public` and `immutable` cookie opt-ins. The existing conservative treatment of shared `proxy-revalidate` also remains. The PR is still open and has no recorded reviews, so this is adoption of a reviewed proposal, not an upstream release. [Patch](https://github.com/kornelski/http-cache-semantics/commit/14a8c2ad51740dc39bf3e8f1a11c845a5003f217), [PR status](https://github.com/kornelski/http-cache-semantics/pull/58)

Use the scoped name and explicit fork version, retain the license, and record the upstream version, commit, patch, and removal condition. Keeping the full source readable is preferable to a compressed artifact, runtime patching, or a misleading upstream version. The roughly 800 lines are the dependency payload.

**The audit qualification must remain explicit.** npm submits package names and versions, which explains why the Git pin still reports vulnerable 4.2.0. A renamed or linked local fork loses automatic association with upstream advisories. Retaining `npm audit --audit-level=high` preserves the registry dependency gate, but a zero result does not validate the fork. Its evidence is the source comparison, review, and behavioral regression. [npm audit documentation](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-audit/), [npm audit implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/npm/cli/latest/workspaces/arborist/lib/audit-report.js)

The regression should load Astro’s resolved dependency and cover both bare and oversized numeric `max-stale` against restricted responses. Controls should preserve ordinary permitted stale reuse, reject insufficient allowances, preserve cookie opt-ins and private-cache behavior, and reject URL or `Vary` mismatches.

I found no separate policy blocker to a transparent, source-backed fork within the authorized repair. Do not describe it as unchanged audit coverage. Record the manual upstream-advisory responsibility and replace it when a suitable upstream release becomes available.

No files changed, dependencies installed, or tests ran.

🟢 Patch review complete. A transparent fork is reasonable with explicit audit limits and regression proof.

The existing cleanup uses the owned live root with `taskkill /T` and checks that the preview port closes. The detached-descendant fixture represents that case.

I recommend changing the production server to `detached: true` on Windows **only if the controlled Electron comparison demonstrates the need**:

- With the current options, killing Electron also kills the server before it records IPC loss, leaving the detached descendant alive.
- With Windows detachment, the server records IPC loss and its bounded fallback removes both server and descendant.

If both observations hold, detaching the server is a narrow correction that lets the existing parent-loss mechanism run. Keep IPC, hidden windows, and the parent’s normal 15-second fallback unchanged. Verify the parent’s normal tree kill still reaches the detached server. A detached fixture alone does not justify that production change.

The existing desktop tests already use `registerHooks` to stub Electron and import the real `main.mjs`. They do not use a VM.

The smallest behavioral regression is to **export the existing `launchServer` function and call it through that harness**. No wrapper or new dependency is needed.

For one test:

1. Stub `node:child_process` only for `main.mjs`, returning an `EventEmitter` child from `fork`.
2. Temporarily select `win32`, then call `launchServer` with fixture paths and a port.
3. Emit `vivary:desktop:bootstrap-needed`, observe the capability handoff, then emit `ready`.
4. Assert that the actual `fork` call received `detached: true`, `windowsHide: true`, the ordinary Node executable, and the existing IPC stdio configuration.
5. Restore the platform and hooks. Give the fake child no real PID so module exit cleanup cannot signal a process.

That binds the regression to the executed production launch call. A source regex would only check spelling, while driving `runDesktop` would require substantially more Electron window and session mocking.

The reported Electron comparison now supports the production detachment change: current options prevented IPC cleanup and left the descendant alive, while detachment allowed the existing fallback to remove both processes. The durable unit test should preserve that launch configuration. Native evidence remains responsible for proving the Windows process behavior.

The red case checks that a run still holds its run lease when its outcome is written. A review round added the fresh reconcile and dispatch cases, that check, the logged release and per-mark failures, the schedule check on the fresh read, and a check that the tick scanned in three cases. After #144 merged into dev, the branch merged dev and regenerated the patch from dev's patch with the same edits. The four `jobs/` files this change edits were byte-identical to the ones reviewed before the merge, and every Core file #144 changed is byte-identical to dev's. A fourth review round made the cases for the held run and the dispatching paired-host mark count the scan's attempt to take the mark's run lease and check that it got none, so each of the five cases shows that its tick reached the mark. It widened the README's Run now limit to any Run now that arrives while a scan holds the automation's run lease, which can follow a run that has just finished. In pinned Node 24.19.0, libuv creates a per-process, non-inheritable Windows job with `KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`. Each non-detached `uv_spawn` child is assigned to that job. Therefore, detaching the server from Electron does not disable the server’s own job for children it subsequently launches. [Pinned libuv implementation](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v24.19.0/deps/uv/src/win/process.c#L65)

There are limits. Libuv enables silent breakaway, so grandchildren do not automatically remain in that job. It also tolerates an access-denied failure when job assignment is incompatible. These limits existed before the server-detachment change. A deliberately escaped descendant surviving a crash does not, by itself, establish a new regression. **No launch-flag-only correction preserves arbitrary supported npm, pnpm, and bun scripts while guaranteeing cleanup of this chain.** The actual-chain Windows regression is the right endpoint for this bounded wave.

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Wrap the package manager in `cmd.exe` | Moves the uncontained hop. Libuv’s silent-breakaway job still covers only explicitly enrolled children. |
| Run the script directly or substitute a shell | Changes package-manager environment, configuration, command resolution, or Windows shell semantics. It does not preserve the existing contract. |
| Reuse Core’s `_WindowsProcessScope` | Has the appropriate containment mechanism, but requires a persistent Python preview owner and a streaming lifecycle bridge. |
| Own a Windows job directly from Node | Requires a native binding or helper that supports suspended creation, job assignment, and resume. That exceeds this wave’s constraints. |

Core’s implementation at `packages/core/vivary_core/workspace_observe.py:231` is materially stronger than libuv’s per-process job. It sets kill-on-close without silent breakaway, creates the child suspended, assigns it to the job, then resumes it. Assignment failure aborts the child.

However, it is a private implementation for bounded commands. Its launch API lacks preview working-directory and window options, and `_capped_run` defaults to a ten-second command with collected output. Reusing it for previews would require an owner that remains alive while the preview runs, plus streaming, exit, and stop handling. Existing code reuse does not remove that architectural change.

My recommendation is to **record the real package-manager-chain regression and stop at the reviewed design boundary**. Keep the production defect unresolved. A future authorized design should first consider extracting the existing Core containment mechanism into a supported preview adapter, rather than duplicating its Win32 logic. That decision needs explicit scope for the persistent process owner and its packaging and lifecycle contract.

Payload:

**Reuse Core’s Windows scope through one Python owner per active preview.** This is the smallest viable containment design identified. It preserves the reviewed package-manager command while fixing the shell-descendant gap.

The implementation scope should be:

- Extract the existing suspended-launch, job-assignment, resume, termination, and wait operations from `_WindowsProcessScope` into a supported low-level API. Add working-directory, hidden-window, and stdio options. Do not duplicate its ctypes implementation or use `_capped_run`, whose ten-second buffered-command contract does not fit previews.
- Spawn the owner through the existing bundled Python, non-detached on Windows. It owns the non-breakaway job for the preview’s lifetime. Server death should kill this direct Python child, closing its job handle and terminating the contained tree.
- Pass the unchanged manager executable, argument array, sanitized environment, and reviewed working directory. Enrollment must finish before the manager resumes. Setup failure must leave no running uncontained command, with no bare-spawn fallback.
- Treat owner EOF or a single Stop command as shutdown. Terminate the job, await its empty state within a bound, then dispose it. Normal Stop must wait for confirmed tree termination.

Use bounded NDJSON frames on stdout for launch-ready, preview output, exit, and error. Keep bridge diagnostics on stderr. This avoids adding Windows-specific control-pipe plumbing. Preview output must be encoded as data, never interpreted as protocol. Stop handling must remain responsive under output backpressure.

The largest integration gaps to settle are:

1. **Readiness and ownership.** Owner-ready means containment succeeded, not that HTTP is ready. Preserve the existing preview probe. Update `Entry.child`, process identity, socket-ancestry verification, and cleanup together so they consistently reference the new owner.
2. **Failure reporting.** A broken pipe, owner crash, malformed frame, or cleanup timeout must leave the preview unavailable. None may become a successful Stop merely because the launcher exited.
3. **Packaging.** Python and Core already ship, but the new bridge and extracted API must be included in the bundle and covered by existing manifest/package checks.

A native Node implementation would avoid the Python bridge but require another native binding or helper for suspended creation and job ownership. Reverting Windows server detachment is not an established fix: it reintroduces the demonstrated Electron-parent-loss failure, and the old configuration has not been shown to clear the server-first preview chain.

Acceptance should turn the real pnpm → cmd → preview → ordinary-child regression green, preserve the 13 existing lifecycle controls, exercise script semantics and output/Stop/startup failures, then verify the exact packaged candidate for server-first death, active-preview normal quit, and active-preview parent loss.

This remains a proposal. The explicit boundary for this wave is reached before implementing the persistent owner.

🟢 Core-reuse scope is defined. Persistent-owner implementation remains outside this bounded wave.

- Create the manager suspended, enroll it in Core’s non-breakaway job, then resume it.
- Wait for the manager, terminate any remaining job members, await cleanup, dispose the job, and exit.
- Report startup or cleanup failure through stderr and a nonzero exit, with no uncontained fallback.

Existing HTTP readiness remains the readiness check. Existing `hardStopWorkerTree` can target the Python owner for Stop. Fatal server exit kills that non-detached owner, closing its job handle. The owner’s PID can remain the root for socket-ancestry verification.

- Review the preview service’s **natural-exit cleanup path**. It must correctly handle an owner that already verified its job empty before exiting, rather than treating an attempted tree kill against its departed PID as the only cleanup evidence.

L24: # Job Objects
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: ## In this article
L30: 
L31: A job object allows groups of processes to be managed as a unit. Job objects are namable, securable, sharable objects that control attributes of the processes associated with them. Operations performed on a job object affect all processes associated with the job object. Examples include enforcing limits such as working set size and process priority or terminating all processes associated with a job.
L32:   * cite5†Creating Jobs L33:   * cite6†Managing Processes in Jobs L34:   * cite7†Job Limits and Notifications L35:   * cite8†Resource Accounting for Jobs L36:   * cite9†Managing Job Objects L37:   * cite10†Managing a Process Tree that Uses Job Objects L38: ## Creating Jobs
L39: 
L40: To create a job object, use the cite11†CreateJobObject function. When the job is created, no processes are associated with the job.
L41: 
L42: To associate a process with a job, use the cite12†AssignProcessToJobObject function. After a process is associated with a job, the association cannot be broken. A process can be associated with more than one job in a hierarchy of nested jobs. For more information, see cite13†Nested Jobs .
L43: Windows 7, Windows Server 2008 R2, Windows XP with SP3, Windows Server 2008, Windows Vista and Windows Server 2003: A process can be associated with only one job. Jobs cannot be nested. The ability to nest jobs was added in Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012.
L44: 
L45: You can specify a security descriptor for a job object when you call the cite11†CreateJobObject function. For more information, see cite14†Job Object Security and Access Rights .
L46: ## Managing Processes in Jobs
L47: 
L48: After a process is associated with a job, by default any child processes it creates using cite15†CreateProcess are also associated with the job. (Child processes created using cite16†Win32_Process.Create are not associated with the job.) This default behavior can be changed by setting the extended limit JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK or JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK for the job.
L49:   * If the job has the extended limit JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK and the parent process was created with the CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB flag, then child processes of the parent process are not associated with the job.
L50:   * If the job has the extended limit JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK, then child processes of any parent process associated with the job are not associated with the job. It is not necessary for parent processes to be created with the CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB flag.
L51: If the job is nested, the breakaway settings of parent jobs in the hierarchy affect whether child processes are associated with another job in the hierarchy. For more information, see cite13†Nested Jobs .
L52: 
L53: To determine if a process is running in a job, use the cite17†IsProcessInJob function.
L54: 
L55: To terminate all processes currently associated with a job object, use the cite18†TerminateJobObject function.
L56: ## Job Limits and Notifications
L57: 
L58: A job can enforce limits such as working set size, process priority, and end-of-job time limit on each process that is associated with the job. If a process associated with a job attempts to increase its working set size or process priority from the limit established by the job, the function calls succeed but are silently ignored. A job can also set limits that trigger a notification when they are exceeded but allow the job to continue to run.
L59: To set limits for a job, use the cite19†SetInformationJobObject function. For a list of possible limits that can be set for a job, see the following topics:
L60: 
L61:   * cite20†JOBOBJECT_BASIC_LIMIT_INFORMATION L62:   * cite21†JOBOBJECT_BASIC_UI_RESTRICTIONS L63:   * cite22†JOBOBJECT_CPU_RATE_CONTROL_INFORMATION L64:   * cite23†JOBOBJECT_EXTENDED_LIMIT_INFORMATION L65:   * cite24†JOBOBJECT_NOTIFICATION_LIMIT_INFORMATION L66: Security limits must be set individually for each process associated with a job object. For more information, see cite25†Process Security and Access Rights .
L67: 
L68: Windows XP with SP3 and Windows Server 2003: The cite19†SetInformationJobObject function can be used to set security limitations for all processes associated with a job object. Starting with Windows Vista, security limits must be set individually for each process associated with a job object.
L69: If the job is nested, parent jobs in the hierarchy influence the limit that is enforced for the job. For more information, see cite13†Nested Jobs .
L70: If the job has an associated I/O completion port, it can receive notifications when certain job limits are exceeded. The system sends messages to the completion port when a limit is exceeded or certain other events occur. To associate a completion port with a job, use the cite19†SetInformationJobObject function with the job object information class JobObjectAssociateCompletionPortInformation and a pointer to a cite26†JOBOBJECT_ASSOCIATE_COMPLETION_PORT structure.
L71: It is best to do this when the job is inactive, to reduce the chance of missing notifications for processes whose states change during the association of the completion port.
L72: All messages are sent directly from the job as if the job had called the cite27†PostQueuedCompletionStatus function. A thread must monitor the completion port using the cite28†GetQueuedCompletionStatus function to pick up the messages. Note that, with the exception of limits set with the JobObjectNotificationLimitInformation information class, delivery of messages to the completion port is not guaranteed; failure of a message to arrive does not necessarily mean that the event did not occur.
L73: Notifications for limits set with JobObjectNotificationLimitInformation are guaranteed to arrive at the completion port. For a list of possible messages, see cite26†JOBOBJECT_ASSOCIATE_COMPLETION_PORT .
L74: ## Resource Accounting for Jobs
L75: 
L76: The job object records basic accounting information for all its associated processes, including those that have terminated. To retrieve this accounting information, use the cite29†QueryInformationJobObject function. For a list of the accounting information that is maintained for a job, see the following topics:
L77: 
L78:   * cite30†JOBOBJECT_BASIC_ACCOUNTING_INFORMATION L79:   * cite31†JOBOBJECT_BASIC_AND_IO_ACCOUNTING_INFORMATION L80: If the job object is nested, accounting information for each child job is aggregated in its parent job. For more information, see cite13†Nested Jobs .
L81: ## Managing Job Objects
L82: 
L83: The state of a job object is set to signaled when all of its processes are terminated because the specified end-of-job time limit has been exceeded. Use cite32†WaitForSingleObject or cite33†WaitForSingleObjectEx to monitor the job object for this event.
L84: 
L85: To obtain a handle for an existing job object, use the cite34†OpenJobObject function and specify the name given to the object when it was created. Only named job objects can be opened.
L86: To close a job object handle, use the cite35†CloseHandle function. The job is destroyed when its last handle has been closed and all associated processes have been terminated. However, if the job has the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE flag specified, closing the last job object handle terminates all associated processes and then destroys the job object itself.
L87: If a nested job has the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE flag specified, closing the last job object handle terminates all processes associated with the job and its child jobs in the hierarchy.
L88: ## Managing a Process Tree that Uses Job Objects
L89: 
L90: Starting with Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012, an application can use cite13†nested jobs to manage a process tree that uses more than one job object. However, an application that must run on Windows 7, Windows Server 2008 R2, or earlier versions of Windows that do not support nested jobs must manage the process tree in other ways.
L91: If a tool must manage a process tree that uses job objects and it is not possible to use nested jobs, both the tool and the members of the process tree must cooperate. Use one of the following options:
L92:   * Use the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK limit. If the tool uses this limit, it cannot monitor an entire process tree. The tool can monitor only the processes it adds to the job. If these processes create child processes, they are not associated with the job. In this option, child processes can be associated with other job objects.
L93:   * Use the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK limit. If the tool uses this limit, it can monitor the entire process tree, except for those processes that any member of the tree explicitly breaks away from the tree. A member of the tree can create a child process in a new job object by calling the cite15†CreateProcess function with the CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB flag, then calling the cite12†AssignProcessToJobObject function. Otherwise, the member must handle cases in which AssignProcessToJobObject fails.
L94: The CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB flag has no effect if the tree is not being monitored by the tool. Therefore, this is the preferred option, but it requires advance knowledge of the processes being monitored.
L95:   * Prevent breakaways of any kind by setting neither the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK nor the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK limit. In this option, the tool can monitor the entire process tree. However, if a child process attempts to associate itself or another child process with a job by calling cite12†AssignProcessToJobObject , the call will fail. If the process was designed to be associated with a specific job, this failure may prevent the process from working properly.

L24: # JOBOBJECT_BASIC_ACCOUNTING_INFORMATION structure (winnt.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Contains basic accounting information for a job object.
L33: ## Syntax
L34: 
L35:     `typedef struct _JOBOBJECT_BASIC_ACCOUNTING_INFORMATION {
L36:       LARGE_INTEGER TotalUserTime;
L37:       LARGE_INTEGER TotalKernelTime;
L38:       LARGE_INTEGER ThisPeriodTotalUserTime;
L39:       LARGE_INTEGER ThisPeriodTotalKernelTime;
L40:       DWORD         TotalPageFaultCount;
L41:       DWORD         TotalProcesses;
L42:       DWORD         ActiveProcesses;
L43:       DWORD         TotalTerminatedProcesses;
L44:     } JOBOBJECT_BASIC_ACCOUNTING_INFORMATION, *PJOBOBJECT_BASIC_ACCOUNTING_INFORMATION;
L45:     `
L46: ## Members
L47: 
L48: `TotalUserTime`
L49: 
L50: The total amount of user-mode execution time for all active processes associated with the job, as well as all terminated processes no longer associated with the job, in 100-nanosecond ticks.
L51: 
L52: `TotalKernelTime`
L53: 
L54: The total amount of kernel-mode execution time for all active processes associated with the job, as well as all terminated processes no longer associated with the job, in 100-nanosecond ticks.
L55: 
L56: `ThisPeriodTotalUserTime`
L57: The total amount of user-mode execution time for all active processes associated with the job (as well as all terminated processes no longer associated with the job) since the last call that set a per-job user-mode time limit, in 100-nanosecond ticks.
L58: 
L59: This member is set to 0 on creation of the job, and each time a per-job user-mode time limit is established.
L60: 
L61: `ThisPeriodTotalKernelTime`
L62: The total amount of kernel-mode execution time for all active processes associated with the job (as well as all terminated processes no longer associated with the job) since the last call that set a per-job kernel-mode time limit, in 100-nanosecond ticks.
L63: 
L64: This member is set to zero on creation of the job, and each time a per-job kernel-mode time limit is established.
L65: 
L66: `TotalPageFaultCount`
L67: The total number of page faults encountered by all active processes associated with the job, as well as all terminated processes no longer associated with the job.
L68: 
L69: `TotalProcesses`
L70: 
L71: The total number of processes associated with the job during its lifetime, including those that have terminated. For example, when a process is associated with a job, but the association fails because of a limit violation, this value is incremented.
L72: 
L73: `ActiveProcesses`
L74: The total number of processes currently associated with the job. When a process is associated with a job, but the association fails because of a limit violation, this value is temporarily incremented. When the terminated process exits and all references to the process are released, this value is decremented.
L75: 
L76: `TotalTerminatedProcesses`
L77: 
L78: The total number of processes terminated because of a limit violation.
L79: ## Requirements
L80: 
L81: Requirement  | Value
L82: --- | ---
L83: Minimum supported client  | Windows XP [desktop apps only]
L84: Minimum supported server  | Windows Server 2003 [desktop apps only]
L85: Header  | winnt.h (include Windows.h)

L24: # TerminateJobObject function (jobapi2.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Terminates all processes currently associated with the job. If the job is nested, this function terminates all processes currently associated with the job and all of its child jobs in the hierarchy.
L33: 
L34: ## Syntax
L35: 
L36:     `BOOL TerminateJobObject(
L37:       [in] HANDLE hJob,
L38:       [in] UINT   uExitCode
L39:     );
L40:     `
L41: ## Parameters
L42: 
L43: `[in] hJob`
L44: 
L45: A handle to the job whose processes will be terminated. The cite5†CreateJobObject or cite6†OpenJobObject function returns this handle. This handle must have the JOB_OBJECT_TERMINATE access right. For more information, see cite7†Job Object Security and Access Rights .
L46: 
L47: The handle for each process in the job object must have the PROCESS_TERMINATE access right. For more information, see cite8†Process Security and Access Rights .
L48: 
L49: `[in] uExitCode`
L50: The exit code to be used by all processes and threads in the job object. Use the cite9†GetExitCodeProcess function to retrieve each process's exit value. Use the cite10†GetExitCodeThread function to retrieve each thread's exit value.
L51: ## Return value
L52: 
L53: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
L54: 
L55: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call cite11†GetLastError .
L56: ## Remarks
L57: 
L58: It is not possible for any of the processes associated with the job to postpone or handle the termination. It is as if cite12†TerminateProcess were called for each process associated with the job.
L59: 
L60: Terminating a nested job additionally terminates all child job objects. Resources used by the terminated jobs are charged up the parent job chain in the hierarchy.
L61: To compile an application that uses this function, define _WIN32_WINNT as 0x0500 or later. For more information, see cite13†Using the Windows Headers .
L62: ## Requirements
L63: 
L64: Requirement  | Value
L65: --- | ---
L66: Minimum supported client  | Windows XP [desktop apps only]
L67: Minimum supported server  | Windows Server 2003 [desktop apps only]
L68: Target Platform  | Windows
L69: Header  | jobapi2.h (include Windows.h, Jobapi2.h)
L70: Library  | Kernel32.lib
L71: DLL  | Kernel32.dll

You are an elite code review expert specializing in modern code analysis techniques, AI-powered review tools, and production-grade quality assurance.

## Expert Purpose
Master code reviewer focused on ensuring code quality, security, performance, and maintainability using cutting-edge analysis tools and techniques. Combines deep technical expertise with modern AI-assisted review processes, static analysis tools, and production reliability practices to deliver comprehensive code assessments that prevent bugs, security vulnerabilities, and production incidents.

## Capabilities

### AI-Powered Code Analysis
- Integration with modern AI review tools (Trag, Bito, Codiga, GitHub Copilot)
- Natural language pattern definition for custom review rules
- Context-aware code analysis using LLMs and machine learning
- Automated pull request analysis and comment generation
- Real-time feedback integration with CLI tools and IDEs
- Custom rule-based reviews with team-specific patterns
- Multi-language AI code analysis and suggestion generation

### Modern Static Analysis Tools
- SonarQube, CodeQL, and Semgrep for comprehensive code scanning
- Security-focused analysis with Snyk, Bandit, and OWASP tools
- Performance analysis with profilers and complexity analyzers
- Dependency vulnerability scanning with npm audit, pip-audit
- License compliance checking and open source risk assessment
- Code quality metrics with cyclomatic complexity analysis
- Technical debt assessment and code smell detection

### Security Code Review
- OWASP Top 10 vulnerability detection and prevention
- Input validation and sanitization review
- Authentication and authorization implementation analysis
- Cryptographic implementation and key management review
- SQL injection, XSS, and CSRF prevention verification
- Secrets and credential management assessment
- API security patterns and rate limiting implementation
- Container and infrastructure security code review

### Performance & Scalability Analysis
- Database query optimization and N+1 problem detection
- Memory leak and resource management analysis
- Caching strategy implementation review
- Asynchronous programming pattern verification
- Load testing integration and performance benchmark review
- Connection pooling and resource limit configuration
- Microservices performance patterns and anti-patterns
- Cloud-native performance optimization techniques

### Configuration & Infrastructure Review
- Production configuration security and reliability analysis
- Database connection pool and timeout configuration review
- Container orchestration and Kubernetes manifest analysis

# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"
- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.

If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with "require_escalated". ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.

## When to request escalation

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)

# Process Handles and Identifiers

Feedback

Summarize this article for me

## In this article

When a new process is created by the CreateProcess function, handles of the new process and its primary thread are returned. These handles are created with full access rights, and — subject to security access checking — can be used in any of the functions that accept thread or process handles. These handles can be inherited by child processes, depending on the inheritance flag specified when they are created. The handles are valid until closed, even after the process or thread they represent has been terminated.

The CreateProcess function also returns an identifier that uniquely identifies the process throughout the system. A process can use the GetCurrentProcessId function to get its own process identifier (also known as the process ID or PID). The identifier is valid from the time the process is created until the process has been terminated. A process can use the Process32First function to obtain the process identifier of its parent process.

If you have a process identifier, you can get the process handle by calling the OpenProcess function. OpenProcess enables you to specify the handle's access rights and whether it can be inherited.

A process can use the GetCurrentProcess function to retrieve a pseudo handle to its own process object. This pseudo handle is valid only for the calling process; it cannot be inherited or duplicated for use by other processes. To get the real handle to the process, call the DuplicateHandle function.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A system process is uniquely identified on the system by its process identifier. Like many Windows resources, a process is also identified by its handle, which might not be unique on the computer. handle windows\system
The name match is case-insensitive and the fragment specified can be anywhere in the paths you are interested in.

## Handle Output

When not in search mode (enabled by specifying a name fragment as a parameter), Handle divides its output into sections for each process it is printing handle information for. Dashed lines are used as a separator, immediately below which you will see the process name and its process id (PID). Beneath the process name are listed handle values (in hexadecimal), the type of object the handle is associated with, and the name of the object if it has one.

When in search mode, Handle prints the process names and id's are listed on the left side and the names of the objects that had a match are on the right.

🟡 Architecture review complete. The EOF lifetime pipe and clean owner exit are sufficient for the proposed minimum. Implementation and native acceptance remain pending.

One required correction: **`WaitForSingleObject(job)` cannot establish ordinary job emptiness.** Microsoft documents the job entering the signaled state when its end-of-job time limit terminates the processes. Replace that wait with bounded polling of `QueryInformationJobObject(JobObjectBasicAccountingInformation).ActiveProcesses == 0`. Query failure or deadline expiry must fail cleanup. [Job Objects](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/job-objects), [Basic accounting information](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winnt/ns-winnt-jobobject_basic_accounting_information)

The minimum reusable API can remain:

- `launch(argv, env, cwd, stdin, stdout, stderr, windows_hide)` creates the process suspended, assigns it to the job, then resumes it.
- `terminate()` requests termination of the entire job.
- `wait_stopped(timeout)` confirms `ActiveProcesses == 0` or raises.
- `dispose()` closes the job handle idempotently.

Keep the existing observation caller’s defaults when extracting the class.

The owner contract is coherent with these implementation requirements:

- Its stdin carries lifetime only. The manager gets `DEVNULL` stdin and cannot retain that lifetime pipe.
- EOF **and read failure** trigger cleanup. A failed daemon reader must not leave the main thread waiting indefinitely.
- Keep the job handle noninheritable. Preserve the existing no-breakaway flags and suspended assignment.
- Exit zero only after job emptiness is confirmed. A manager failure can be logged separately, because the owner’s exit status represents cleanup.
- Node attaches exit/error observation before closing stdin, continues draining output, and accepts cleanup only on exit code zero without a terminating signal. The port must also be closed before retiring the preview.
- Cleanup deadlines must leave room inside the existing 15-second parent fallback. A timeout must retain the unresolved owner state rather than report a successful Stop.

One native proof detail remains: Microsoft describes `ActiveProcesses` decrementing after the process exits and its references are released. Test polling with Python’s `Popen` process handle still held. I found no sufficient evidence to require manual handle closure, so do not introduce that preemptively. [Basic accounting information](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winnt/ns-winnt-jobobject_basic_accounting_information)

No further architectural blocker identified. No source changes or tests performed.

- Cleanup deadlines must leave room inside the existing 15-second parent fallback. A timeout must retain the unresolved owner state rather than report a successful Stop.

One native proof detail remains: Microsoft describes `ActiveProcesses` decrementing after the process exits and its references are released. Test polling with Python’s `Popen` process handle still held. I found no sufficient evidence to require manual handle closure, so do not introduce that preemptively. """Native ownership checks for the shared Windows Job scope."""

import ctypes
import os
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import sys
import time

import pytest

from vivary_core.windows_process_scope import WindowsProcessScope

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(os.name != "nt", reason="requires native Windows Job semantics")


def test_scope_stops_descendants_with_the_popen_handle_still_held(tmp_path):
    producer = tmp_path / "producer.py"
    producer.write_text(
        "import os, subprocess, sys\n"
        "assert sys.stdin.buffer.read() == b''\n"
        "assert os.environ['PREVIEW_SCOPE_TEST'] == 'preserved'\n"
        "assert os.getcwd() == sys.argv[1]\n"
        "os.write(1, b'raw-out\\x00\\xff\\n')\n"
        "os.write(2, b'raw-err\\x00\\xfe\\n')\n"
        "subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', 'import time; time.sleep(120)'], "
        "stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, stdout=sys.stdout, stderr=sys.stderr)\n"
    )
    scope = WindowsProcessScope.launch(
        [sys.executable, str(producer), str(tmp_path)],
        {**os.environ, "PREVIEW_SCOPE_TEST": "preserved"}, cwd=str(tmp_path),
        stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, windows_hide=True,
    )
    try:
        assert scope.proc.wait(timeout=5) == 0
        assert getattr(scope.proc, "_handle", None) is not None
        # The parent ended but its pipe-holding descendant remains a live job member.
        with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="cleanup timed out"):
            scope.wait_stopped(time.monotonic() + 0.1)
        scope.terminate()
        scope.wait_stopped(time.monotonic() + 3)
        # Keep Popen's native process handle open throughout the accounting query.
        assert getattr(scope.proc, "_handle", None) is not None
        stdout, stderr = scope.proc.communicate(timeout=3)
        assert stdout == b"raw-out\x00\xff\n"
        assert stderr == b"raw-err\x00\xfe\n"
    finally:
        scope.dispose()


def test_failed_assignment_aborts_the_suspended_child_before_it_executes(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    marker = tmp_path / "must-not-run"
    original_loader = ctypes.WinDLL
    kernel = original_loader("kernel32", use_last_error=True)

    def refuse_assignment(*_args):
        ctypes.set_last_error(5)
        return 0

    kernel.AssignProcessToJobObject = refuse_assignment
    monkeypatch.setattr(ctypes, "WinDLL", lambda name, **options:
                        kernel if name == "kernel32" else original_loader(name, **options))
    original_popen = subprocess.Popen
    started = []

    def observe_popen(*args, **options):
        process = original_popen(*args, **options)
        started.append(process)
        return process

    monkeypatch.setattr(subprocess, "Popen", observe_popen)
    command = [sys.executable, "-c", "from pathlib import Path; import sys; Path(sys.argv[1]).touch()", str(marker)]
    with pytest.raises(OSError, match="AssignProcessToJobObject"):
        WindowsProcessScope.launch(command, dict(os.environ), stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, windows_hide=True)
    assert len(started) == 1
    assert started[0].poll() is not None, "the rejected suspended child was reaped"
    assert not marker.exists(), "the child never ran before containment was established"

import ctypes
import os
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import sys
import time

import pytest

from vivary_core.windows_process_scope import WindowsProcessScope

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(os.name != "nt", reason="requires native Windows Job semantics")


def test_scope_stops_descendants_with_the_popen_handle_still_held(tmp_path):
    producer = tmp_path / "producer.py"
    producer.write_text(
        "import os, subprocess, sys\n"
        "assert sys.stdin.buffer.read() == b''\n"
        "assert os.environ['PREVIEW_SCOPE_TEST'] == 'preserved'\n"
        "assert os.getcwd() == sys.argv[1]\n"
        "os.write(1, b'raw-out\\x00\\xff\\n')\n"
        "os.write(2, b'raw-err\\x00\\xfe\\n')\n"
        "subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', 'import time; time.sleep(120)'], "
        "stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, stdout=sys.stdout, stderr=sys.stderr)\n"
    )
    scope = WindowsProcessScope.launch(
        [sys.executable, str(producer), str(tmp_path)],
        {**os.environ, "PREVIEW_SCOPE_TEST": "preserved"}, cwd=str(tmp_path),
        stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, windows_hide=True,
    )
    try:
        assert scope.proc.wait(timeout=5) == 0
        assert getattr(scope.proc, "_handle", None) is not None
        # The parent ended but its pipe-holding descendant remains a live job member.
        with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="cleanup timed out"):
            scope.wait_stopped(time.monotonic() + 0.1)
        scope.terminate()
        scope.wait_stopped(time.monotonic() + 3)
        # Keep Popen's native process handle open throughout the accounting query.
        assert getattr(scope.proc, "_handle", None) is not None
        stdout, stderr = scope.proc.communicate(timeout=3)
        assert stdout == b"raw-out\x00\xff\n"
        assert stderr == b"raw-err\x00\xfe\n"
    finally:
        scope.dispose()


def test_failed_assignment_aborts_the_suspended_child_before_it_executes(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    marker = tmp_path / "must-not-run"
    original_loader = ctypes.WinDLL
    kernel = original_loader("kernel32", use_last_error=True)

    def refuse_assignment(*_args):
        ctypes.set_last_error(5)
        return 0

    kernel.AssignProcessToJobObject = refuse_assignment
    monkeypatch.setattr(ctypes, "WinDLL", lambda name, **options:
                        kernel if name == "kernel32" else original_loader(name, **options))
    original_popen = subprocess.Popen
    started = []

    def observe_popen(*args, **options):
        process = original_popen(*args, **options)
        started.append(process)
        return process

    monkeypatch.setattr(subprocess, "Popen", observe_popen)
    command = [sys.executable, "-c", "from pathlib import Path; import sys; Path(sys.argv[1]).touch()", str(marker)]
    with pytest.raises(OSError, match="AssignProcessToJobObject"):
        WindowsProcessScope.launch(command, dict(os.environ), stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, windows_hide=True)
    assert len(started) == 1
    assert started[0].poll() is not None, "the rejected suspended child was reaped"
    assert not marker.exists(), "the child never ran before containment was established"

import ctypes
import os
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import sys
import time

import pytest

from vivary_core.windows_process_scope import WindowsProcessScope

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(os.name != "nt", reason="requires native Windows Job semantics")


def test_scope_stops_descendants_with_the_popen_handle_still_held(tmp_path):
    producer = tmp_path / "producer.py"
    producer.write_text(
        "import os, subprocess, sys\n"
        "assert sys.stdin.buffer.read() == b''\n"
        "assert os.environ['PREVIEW_SCOPE_TEST'] == 'preserved'\n"
        "assert os.getcwd() == sys.argv[1]\n"
        "os.write(1, b'raw-out\\x00\\xff\\n')\n"
        "os.write(2, b'raw-err\\x00\\xfe\\n')\n"
        "subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', 'import time; time.sleep(120)'], "
        "stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, stdout=sys.stdout, stderr=sys.stderr)\n"
    )
    scope = WindowsProcessScope.launch(
        [sys.executable, str(producer), str(tmp_path)],
        {**os.environ, "PREVIEW_SCOPE_TEST": "preserved"}, cwd=str(tmp_path),
        stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, windows_hide=True,
    )
    try:
        assert scope.proc.wait(timeout=5) == 0
        assert getattr(scope.proc, "_handle", None) is not None
        # The parent ended but its pipe-holding descendant remains a live job member.
        with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="cleanup timed out"):
            scope.wait_stopped(time.monotonic() + 0.1)
        scope.terminate()
        scope.wait_stopped(time.monotonic() + 3)
        # Keep Popen's native process handle open throughout the accounting query.
        assert getattr(scope.proc, "_handle", None) is not None
        stdout, stderr = scope.proc.communicate(timeout=3)
        assert stdout == b"raw-out\x00\xff\n"
        assert stderr == b"raw-err\x00\xfe\n"
    finally:
        scope.dispose()


def test_failed_assignment_aborts_the_suspended_child_before_it_executes(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    marker = tmp_path / "must-not-run"
    original_loader = ctypes.WinDLL
    kernel = original_loader("kernel32", use_last_error=True)

    def refuse_assignment(*_args):
        ctypes.set_last_error(5)
        return 0

    kernel.AssignProcessToJobObject = refuse_assignment
    monkeypatch.setattr(ctypes, "WinDLL", lambda name, **options:
                        kernel if name == "kernel32" else original_loader(name, **options))
    original_popen = subprocess.Popen
    started = []

    def observe_popen(*args, **options):
        process = original_popen(*args, **options)
        started.append(process)
        return process

    monkeypatch.setattr(subprocess, "Popen", observe_popen)
    command = [sys.executable, "-c", "from pathlib import Path; import sys; Path(sys.argv[1]).touch()", str(marker)]
    with pytest.raises(OSError, match="AssignProcessToJobObject"):
        WindowsProcessScope.launch(command, dict(os.environ), stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, windows_hide=True)
    assert len(started) == 1
    assert started[0].poll() is not None, "the rejected suspended child was reaped"
    assert not marker.exists(), "the child never ran before containment was established"

"""Native ownership checks for the shared Windows Job scope."""

import ctypes
import os
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import sys
import time

import pytest

from vivary_core.windows_process_scope import WindowsProcessScope

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(os.name != "nt", reason="requires native Windows Job semantics")


def test_scope_stops_descendants_with_the_popen_handle_still_held(tmp_path):
    producer = tmp_path / "producer.py"
    producer.write_text(
        "import os, subprocess, sys\n"
        "assert sys.stdin.buffer.read() == b''\n"
        "assert os.environ['PREVIEW_SCOPE_TEST'] == 'preserved'\n"
        "assert os.getcwd() == sys.argv[1]\n"
        "os.write(1, b'raw-out\\x00\\xff\\n')\n"
        "os.write(2, b'raw-err\\x00\\xfe\\n')\n"
        "subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', 'import time; time.sleep(120)'], "
        "stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, stdout=sys.stdout, stderr=sys.stderr)\n"
    )
    scope = WindowsProcessScope.launch(
        [sys.executable, str(producer), str(tmp_path)],
        {**os.environ, "PREVIEW_SCOPE_TEST": "preserved"}, cwd=str(tmp_path),
        stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, windows_hide=True,
    )
    try:
        assert scope.proc.wait(timeout=5) == 0
        assert getattr(scope.proc, "_handle", None) is not None
        # The parent ended but its pipe-holding descendant remains a live job member.
        with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="cleanup timed out"):
            scope.wait_stopped(time.monotonic() + 0.1)
        scope.terminate()
        scope.wait_stopped(time.monotonic() + 3)
        # Keep Popen's native process handle open throughout the accounting query.
        assert getattr(scope.proc, "_handle", None) is not None
        stdout, stderr = scope.proc.communicate(timeout=3)
        assert stdout == b"raw-out\x00\xff\n"
        assert stderr == b"raw-err\x00\xfe\n"
    finally:
        scope.dispose()


def test_failed_assignment_aborts_the_suspended_child_before_it_executes(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    marker = tmp_path / "must-not-run"
    original_loader = ctypes.WinDLL
    kernel = original_loader("kernel32", use_last_error=True)

    def refuse_assignment(*_args):
        ctypes.set_last_error(5)
        return 0

    kernel.AssignProcessToJobObject = refuse_assignment
    monkeypatch.setattr(ctypes, "WinDLL", lambda name, **options:
                        kernel if name == "kernel32" else original_loader(name, **options))
    original_popen = subprocess.Popen
    started = []

    def observe_popen(*args, **options):
        process = original_popen(*args, **options)
        started.append(process)
        return process

    monkeypatch.setattr(subprocess, "Popen", observe_popen)
    command = [sys.executable, "-c", "from pathlib import Path; import sys; Path(sys.argv[1]).touch()", str(marker)]
    with pytest.raises(OSError, match="AssignProcessToJobObject"):
        WindowsProcessScope.launch(command, dict(os.environ), stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, windows_hide=True)
    assert len(started) == 1
    assert started[0].poll() is not None, "the rejected suspended child was reaped"
    assert not marker.exists(), "the child never ran before containment was established"
"}

The final pipe-error fix closes the identified race:

- `project-preview.ts:28` observes owner exit, child errors, and stdin errors immediately after spawn.
- `project-preview.ts:416` makes Stop await confirmed owner cleanup, including failed launches without a PID, and clears the timeout.
- `project-preview.ts:677` uses the same cleanup promise for natural exit before checking the port and retiring ownership.

The Core extraction preserves suspended launch, job assignment, resume, and kill-on-close containment. Its accounting structure and `QueryInformationJobObject` bindings match the intended active-process query. The owner handles EOF and read errors, preserves manager cwd/environment/raw output, and reports success only after verified job emptiness.

Packaging copies and hashes the new bridge. The held-process-handle and failed-assignment tests are included in the existing Windows Core test job.

🟡 Native Windows results and packaged acceptance remain required. I performed no edits or tests.

param(
  [Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$LaunchLabel,
  [Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$Label
)
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
if ($LaunchLabel -notmatch '^[a-z0-9-]+$' -or $Label -notmatch '^[a-z0-9-]+$') { throw 'Invalid evidence label' }
$launch = Get-Content -Raw -LiteralPath (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "evidence\launch-$LaunchLabel.json") | ConvertFrom-Json
$application = Get-Process -Id $launch.Pid -ErrorAction Stop
if ($application.Path -ne $launch.Executable) { throw 'The launch process identity changed' }
$candidateRoot = [System.IO.Path]::GetDirectoryName($launch.Executable)
$resolvedRoot = [System.IO.Path]::GetFullPath($candidateRoot)
$acceptanceRoot = [System.IO.Path]::GetFullPath($PSScriptRoot) + '\'
if (-not $resolvedRoot.StartsWith($acceptanceRoot, [System.StringComparison]::OrdinalIgnoreCase)) { throw 'Candidate is outside acceptance setup' }
$before = @(Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object { $_.ExecutablePath -and $_.ExecutablePath.StartsWith($resolvedRoot + '\', [System.StringComparison]::OrdinalIgnoreCase) } | Select-Object ProcessId,ParentProcessId,Name,CreationDate)
$started = (Get-Date).ToUniversalTime().ToString('o')
$timer = [System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch]::StartNew()
$closeSent = $application.CloseMainWindow()
if (-not $closeSent) { throw 'The app did not accept a normal window close request' }
$mainExited = $application.WaitForExit(25000)
$mainMilliseconds = $timer.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds
$mainExitedAt = if ($mainExited) { (Get-Date).ToUniversalTime().ToString('o') } else { $null }
$remaining = @()
do {
  $remaining = @(Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object { $_.ExecutablePath -and $_.ExecutablePath.StartsWith($resolvedRoot + '\', [System.StringComparison]::OrdinalIgnoreCase) } | Select-Object ProcessId,ParentProcessId,Name,CreationDate)
  if ($remaining.Count -eq 0) { break }
  Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 100
} while ($timer.Elapsed.TotalSeconds -lt 30)
$timer.Stop()
$result = [pscustomobject]@{
  Label = $Label
  SourceCommit = $launch.SourceCommit
  MainPid = $launch.Pid
  CloseRequestedAt = $started
  CloseSent = $closeSent
  MainExited = $mainExited
  MainExitedAt = $mainExitedAt
  MainExitMilliseconds = [Math]::Round($mainMilliseconds, 2)
  AllCandidateProcessesGone = ($remaining.Count -eq 0)
  AllGoneMilliseconds = [Math]::Round($timer.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds, 2)
  Before = $before
  Remaining = $remaining
}
$json = $result | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText((Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "evidence\quit-$Label.json"), $json + "`n", [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false))
$json
if (-not $mainExited -or $remaining.Count -ne 0) { throw 'Normal close left candidate processes alive' }
